introduction: Evanescence and permanence, faná and baqá in the language of the Sufis, name a single movement: the self recedes, its will is lost in the will of God, and what remains is said to be the only life that lasts. The readings take the terms from Persian mysticism and bend them toward servitude and humility: to be evanescent is to serve without name, to prefer the consuming of the candle to its burning, to count fame and oblivion as one. Jesus on losing one's life, Paul's not I, the Qur’an's verse that all passes save the countenance of God, Lao Tzu, Rumi and Rabia stand beside them. Emerson, Whitman, Henley, Tagore and the Dhammapada speak for the self that is to be trusted, sung, mastered or kept, and several quotations ask when the language of nothingness heals and when it harms.
questions: What exactly passes away in evanescence, on these readings, and what remains?
The readings say no one's will is ever united with God's, yet ask that one's will be annihilated in his. How does that differ from what Hallaj claimed?
The psalmist calls himself a worm; Leviticus assumes one loves oneself. When is the language of nothingness healthy, and what guards it from self-contempt?
Whitman sings himself and Henley captains his soul. What would each lose, and what might each gain, by the readings' counsel?
How do the readings turn evanescence into a way of working with others: without titles, without fame, of one voice?

outside.why: Jesus begins his sermon by blessing the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Paul describes himself as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.
Jesus says that whoever will save his life shall lose it, and whoever loses it for his sake shall find it.
John the Baptist says of the one he announced: he must increase, but I must decrease.
In the garden Jesus prays: not my will, but thine, be done.
Dante's blessed soul says it is the essence of that life to keep within the divine will, and his will is our peace.
Isaiah counts the nations as a drop of a bucket and the small dust of the balance.
Hallaj sang: I am He whom I love, and He whom I love is I. Does the reading leave any room for the union this Sufi claimed?
The psalm crowns man with glory and honour, a little lower than the angels. How do the readings hold human nothingness and human dignity together?
The Lord's Prayer asks that God's will be done in earth as it is in heaven.
Rabia gives away her share of this world and the next: thou art enough for me.
Ignatius prays: take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my intellect and all my will.
Emerson, standing on bare ground, says all mean egotism vanishes: I am nothing; I see all.
The psalm gives the stillness of this station in a line: be still, and know that I am God.
Paul asks believers to present their bodies a living sacrifice, which is their reasonable service.
Emerson says, trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string. Is effacement the loss of that self, or its truest use?
Paul protests in four words what the reading asks of those who belong to God: I die daily.
Jesus says, I can of mine own self do nothing: I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father.
Henley declares, I am the master of my fate, I am the captain of my soul. What does each view fear in the other?
Wollstonecraft wanted minds enlarged so that blind obedience would end. How is a will annihilated in God's will different from a will given up to another person?
Paul says: I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me.
Donne asks God to batter his heart, for he shall never be free unless God enthral him.
Jesus says the wind blows where it lists, and so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
The psalmist asks that the words of his mouth and the meditation of his heart be acceptable.
Jesus says that whoever would be chiefest shall be servant of all.
Jesus washes his disciples' feet and tells Peter that otherwise he has no part with him.
Jesus teaches his followers to say, when all is done: we are unprofitable servants; we have done our duty.
Paul says Christ made himself of no reputation and took upon him the form of a servant.
The psalmist calls himself a worm and no man, despised of the people. When is such language health, and when is it harm?
Leviticus asks love of neighbour as thyself, which supposes a self that may be loved. What place has that in a teaching of self-effacement?
Whitman celebrates and sings himself. Is the sense of one's own distinct existence a fault, as the reading says, or something to be offered?
Gray thinks of the gem in the ocean cave and the flower born to blush unseen.
George Eliot holds that the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts.
Jesus says of giving: let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth.
Jesus tells his disciples to refuse the titles Rabbi and master, for all ye are brethren.
Jesus advises the guest at a feast to take the lowest room and not the highest.
Herbert asks to do everything as for God, which makes drudgery divine.
Tagore says that infinite gifts come to him only on very small hands, and still there is room to fill.
Jeremiah says the word was in his heart as a burning fire shut up in his bones.
Micah says what the Lord requires: to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.
Franklin found that had he overcome pride, he would probably be proud of his humility. How is self-effacement taught without becoming a new distinction?
Paul asks his friends to be of one accord, of one mind.
Mary answers the angel with the words of a servant: behold the handmaid of the Lord.
Paul says the treasure is in earthen vessels, that the power may be of God and not of us.
Isaiah hears the question, whom shall I send, and answers, here am I; send me.
The psalmist prays: open thou my lips, and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise.
Job falls to the ground and says: naked came I, and naked shall I return.
The Qur’an says that in the remembrance of God hearts find rest.
Jesus says: lay not up treasures upon earth, where moth and rust corrupt.
Paul counts all he had gained as loss, and all things as loss beside what he has found.
An Upanishad says the rivers, when they reach the sea, no longer know themselves as this or that river.
The Dhammapada says self is the lord of self; who else could be the lord? Is the self to be lost, or mastered?
Jesus says a corn of wheat abides alone unless it die, and if it die it brings forth much fruit.
Ignatius of Antioch calls himself the wheat of God, to be ground by the teeth of wild beasts into pure bread.
Jesus says there is no greater love than to lay down one's life for one's friends.
Shelley writes that the One remains while the many change and pass.
Tagore says deliverance is not for him in renunciation: he feels freedom in a thousand bonds of delight. Must this world's life be released to find what the reading seeks?
Lao Tzu says the sage puts his own person last, and yet it is found in the foremost place.
Lao Tzu says that he who dies and yet does not perish has longevity.
Plato's prisoners take shadows on a wall for the things themselves, and pursue nothing else.
Paul says the things which are seen are temporal, but the things not seen are eternal.
Paul says: ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God.
The psalmist wishes for wings like a dove, to fly away and be at rest.
Paul says the things of the Spirit are spiritually discerned, and the natural man cannot know them.
Marcus Aurelius quotes Epictetus: thou art a little soul bearing about a corpse.
Isaiah is told to cry that all flesh is grass, and its goodliness as the flower of the field.
Pascal calls man a nothing in comparison with the infinite, and an all in comparison with the nothing.
The psalm says the heavens shall perish and wax old like a garment, but thou shalt endure.
The Qur’an says that everything will perish save his countenance, and unto him all are brought back.
Julian is shown all that is made as a little thing like a hazel nut, and marvels that it lasts.
The psalmist asks whom he has in heaven but God, and desires none on earth beside him.
The Qur’an gives the two words of this guide in one verse: all passes, and there remains the countenance of thy Lord.
Augustine confesses that he sought outside what was within him all the while.
The Song of Songs says that love is strong as death, the station the reading names.
Proverbs praises one who rules his spirit above one who takes a city. Is the highest state the mastery of anger, or its absence?
Jesus tells Simon he has prayed for him, that his faith fail not.
Lucretius cured the fear of non-existence by another road: what was before our birth was nothing to us. What different comfort do the readings offer?
Hamlet puts the fear into a question: to be, or not to be.
The Preacher looked on all the works his hands had wrought, and behold, all was vanity.
Shelley's traveller finds a king's boast on a wrecked statue, and nothing beside remains.
Augustine says that we are made for God, and our hearts are restless until they rest in him.
Paul is in a strait between two, having a desire to depart and be with Christ.
The psalmist says: return unto thy rest, O my soul, for the Lord hath dealt bountifully.
Thomas à Kempis says love is a great thing that makes everything heavy light.
Rumi tells his dyings one by one, as mineral, plant and animal, each a rising to something more.
The Tao Te Ching opens by saying that the name that can be named is not the enduring name.
Paul speaks of a savour of knowledge made manifest in every place.
Paul says: be not drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit.
FitzGerald's Omar asks only a jug of wine, a book of verses and Thou. How do the Persian poets, and these readings, make the tavern a figure for something else?
At Pentecost mockers say the disciples are full of new wine, and Peter answers that they are not drunk.
Zechariah is told: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
Paul says that knowledge puffs up, but charity edifies, a warning to the learned.
Bacon held that studies serve for delight, for ornament and for ability. Is devotion to learning a lesser road than evanescence, or one of its forms?
Jesus says that the Son of man has not where to lay his head.
Rumi's reed laments its banishment from the reed-bed and longs to return.
The psalmist's soul thirsts for God in a dry and thirsty land.

quran-countenance-of-thy-lord-remaineth.text: There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory.

quran-everyone-that-is-thereon-will-pass.text: Everyone that is thereon will pass away;

matthew-deny-himself-and-take-up-his-cro.text: Then said Jesus unto his disciples, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it

corinthians-i-die-daily.text: I protest by your rejoicing which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die daily

psalm-i-am-a-worm-and-no-man.text: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people

tao-puts-his-own-person-last.text: Therefore the sage puts his own person last, and yet it is found in the foremost place; he treats his person as if it were foreign to him, and yet that person is preserved. Is it not because he has no personal and private ends, that therefore such ends are realised
